title: LCIA Challenge Decision — Decision 8 (20/02/2019)
text:
DECISION RENDERED ON 20 FEBRUARY 2019
Subject: The Claimant challenged one of the Arbitrators (appointed by the
Respondents) pursuant to Article 11(1) of the UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules
1976.
Outcome: Rejected
Seat: Paris, France
Governing Law of Brazilian law
the Contract:
Summary: The challenge related to the Arbitrator’s: (i) previous relationship with a law
firm which had represented affiliates of one of the Respondents; (ii)
membership in the industry association responsible for drafting a relevant
standard form agreement; (iii) involvement in the drafting of an earlier version
of a standard form agreement; and (iv) failure to disclose some of these
circumstances.
The Claimant contended that the foregoing matters called into question the
Arbitrator's independence and impartiality in the arbitration, particularly
because the Arbitrator worked in a firm that provided services to, and
received substantial fees from, the Second Respondent's owners. In addition,
the Claimant argued that the Arbitrator’s work in drafting the standard form
agreement caused the Arbitrator to be biased in relation to participating in
the decision-making process about the validity of clauses of a contract that
were based on that model.
The LCIA Court rejected the challenge.
The fact of non-disclosure cannot, of itself, give rise to justifiable doubts as to
impartiality if the undisclosed facts themselves are insufficient to ground a
proper challenge.
Even where the facts fall squarely within one of the scenarios in the Orange
List of the IBA Conflicts Guidelines, disqualification is not automatic and, as
the General Standards state, the outcome depends on the particular facts. The
question to be decided is whether, viewed objectively, those facts give rise to
justifiable doubts as to the Arbitrator’s impartiality.
Regarding paragraphs 3.1.1 or 3.1.4 of the Orange List of the IBA Conflicts
Guidelines, it is relevant to consider whether the event relied on is close to
falling outside the three-year period under those paragraphs and therefore
whether it is cured by the passing of time.

The fact that a law firm associated with the firm which the Arbitrator
previously worked for had represented affiliates of one of the Respondents
does not justify the conclusion that the Arbitrator lacked impartiality,
considering the time elapsed since the Arbitrator left the firm (approximately
2.5 years), the tentative nature of the connection between the Arbitrator and
the relevant companies, and the Arbitrator’s ignorance of the companies in
question.
Thus, the mere fact that some connection may exist between an arbitrator
and the parties or personnel involved in an arbitration is not of itself a matter
of criticism and is unlikely of itself to be sufficient to disqualify a prospective
arbitrator.
While there may be a duty by a prospective arbitrator to investigate whether
a law firm for which the prospective arbitrator has worked in the past has
acted for the parties to the case or for known associates of those companies,
it is difficult to see how the duty could extend to companies of which the
prospective arbitrator is unaware.
The fact that the Arbitrator is a member (which was disclosed at the time of
nomination) of an association responsible for drafting the standard form
agreements upon which the agreement in dispute was based, and that the
Arbitrator had some involvement – more than 20 years ago – in the drafting
of an earlier version of the standard form agreement, also fail as a ground for
challenge. The length of time that has elapsed since the Arbitrator’s
involvement in drafting the standard forms is such as to render any prejudice
to the Claimant of questionable significance. Of even more relevance is that
the Arbitrator’s involvement with the association was disclosed alongside the
Arbitrator’s website where further details were readily available. If further
information as to the Arbitrator’s work in the earlier version of the form and
thereafter with the association was regarded as relevant it could have been
requested at the nomination stage, but it was not.
Decision 8 - 2

LONDON COURT OF INTERNATIONAL ARBITRATION
ARBITRATION N. […]
[…]
Claimant:
AND
[...]
First Respondent
[...]
Second Respondent
_________________________________________________________
DECISION ON CLAIMANT'S CHALLENGE TO [A]
_________________________________________________________________
Introduction
1. The relevant contract giving rise to the present dispute [(the Agreement)] […] was originally executed
on 22 December 2000 among other parties and subsequently amended on various occasions to
include and/or exclude other parties, resulting in the present Claimant and Respondents being the
relevant parties at the date of initiation of the present arbitral proceedings. (Emphasis added).
2. The parties at the date of the initiation of the arbitration are the following:
The Claimant is: […] a company […];
The First Respondent is: [...] a company […]; and
The Second Respondent is: […] a company […].
3. The present arbitration was initiated on 20 October 2017 between the aforesaid parties. The
arbitration rules applicable are the UNCITRAL Rules in effect as of the effective date of the
Decision 8 - 3

[Agreement], namely the 1976 UNCITRAL Rules. Pursuant to the arbitration agreement and the Rules,
the Tribunal is to consist of two co-arbitrators, one to be appointed by each party or group of parties,
and a presiding arbitrator to be appointed by the two party-appointed arbitrators or an appointing
authority. Pursuant to the arbitration agreement and the UNCITRAL Rules the Appointing Authority is
the chairperson or equivalent of the LCIA; the arbitration proceeding are to be administered by the
LCIA; the seat of arbitration is Paris, France; the arbitration proceedings are to be conducted in English;
and the arbitrators are to be and remain at all times wholly independent and impartial.
4. The [Agreement] is to be governed by, construed, interpreted and applied in accordance with the laws
of the República Federativa do Brasil, excluding any choice of law rules which would refer the matter
to the laws of any other jurisdiction. 1
5. Pursuant to Article 12.1(b) of the UNCITRAL Rules, if the other parties do not all agree to the challenge
and if the challenged arbitrator does not withdraw, the decision on the challenge is to be made by the
appointing authority, namely […] the London Court of International Arbitration. The Claimant having
brought the present challenge to [A] and such challenge not having been accepted either by the other
parties or by [A], the challenge now falls to be determined.
6. On 24 January 2019, the LCIA Secretariat notified the undersigned that he had been selected by the
LCIA Court, […], to determine the challenge, subject to completion of a Statement of Independence.
Such statement having been provided, the parties were on 25 January 2019 notified of my
appointment.
7. Having now had the opportunity to study the challenge and the various responses referred to below,
this Decision summarises the issues raised by the challenge and the responses thereto and sets out
my conclusions on those issues.
Rules aspplicable to the challenge
8. By the UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules 1976
Challenge of the Arbitrators
1 clause 18.1 of the [Agreement]
Decision 8 - 4

Article 9
A prospective arbitrator shall disclose to those who approach him in connection with his possible
appointment any circumstances likely to give rise to justifiable doubts as to his impartiality and
independence. An arbitrator once appointed or chosen shall disclose such circumstances to the parties
unless they have already been informed by him of these.
Article 10
Any arbitrator may be challenged if circumstances exist that give rise to justifiable doubts as to the
arbitrator’s impartiality or independence.
Article 11.1
A party who intends to challenge an arbitrator shall send notice of his challenge within 15 days after
the appointment of the challenged arbitrator has been notified to the challenging party or within 15
days after the circumstances mentioned in Articles 9 and 10 became known to that party.
Article 12
If the other party does not agree to the challenge and the challenged arbitrator does not withdraw
the decision on the challenge will made:
(a) When the initial appointment was made by an appointing authority, by that authority.
9. By the IBA Guidelines on Conflicts of Interest in International Arbitration, 2014
Part I, General Standards
(1) General Principle
Every arbitrator shall be impartial and independent of the parties at the time of accepting an
appointment to serve and shall remain so until the final award has been rendered or the proceedings
are otherwise finally terminated.
(4) Waiver by the Parties
If within 30 days after the receipt of any disclosure by the arbitrator, or after a party otherwise learns
a fact or circumstances that could constitute a potential conflict of interest for an arbitrator, a party
does not raise an express objection with regard to that arbitrator, …. the party is deemed to have
waived any potential conflict of interest in respect of the arbitrator based on such facts or
circumstances and may not raise any objection based on such facts or circumstances at a later stage.
(7) Duty of parties and the arbitrator
Decision 8 - 5

(a) A party shall inform an arbitrator, the Arbitral Tribunal, the other parties and the arbitration
institution or other appointing authority (if any) of any relationship, direct or indirect, between the
arbitrator and the party (or another company of the same group of companies, or an individual having
a controlling influence on the party in the arbitration), or between the arbitrator and any person or
entity with a direct economic interest in, or a duty to indemnify a party for, the award to be rendered
in the arbitration. The party shall do so on its own initiative at the earliest opportunity.
(c) In order to comply with General Standard 7(a) a party shall perform reasonable inquires and
provide any information reasonably available to it.
(d) An arbitrator is under a duty to make reasonable enquiries to identify any conflict of interest, as
well as any facts or circumstances that may reasonably give rise to doubts as to his or her impartiality
or independence. Failure to disclose a conflict is not excused by lack of knowledge, if the arbitrator
does not perform such reasonable enquiries.
Part II: Practical Application of General Standards
(3) The Orange List is a non-exhaustive list of specific situations that, depending on the facts of the
given case, may in the eyes of the parties, give rise to doubts as to the arbitrator’s impartiality or
independence. The Orange List thus reflects situations that would fall under General Standard 3(a)
with the consequence that the arbitrator has a duty to disclose such situations. In all these situations
the parties are deemed to have accepted the arbitrator if, after this disclosure, no timely objection is
made as established in General Standard 4(a).
Orange List
3.1 Previous services for one of the parties or other involvement in the case.
3.1.1 The arbitrator has within the past 3 years served as Counsel for one of the parties or an affiliate
of one of the parties or has previously advised or been consulted by the party or an affiliate of the
party making the appointment in an unrelated matter but the arbitrator and the party or the affiliate
of the party had no ongoing relationship.
3.1.4 The arbitrator’s law firm has, within the past 3 years, acted for or against one of the parties or
an affiliate of one of the parties, in an unrelated matter without the involvement of the arbitrator.
Background to Claimant's Challenge
10. In November, 2017, [A] was jointly nominated by the Respondents as their co-arbitrator. Upon
nomination [A] submitted, with his Statement of Independence and Consent to Appointment dated
27 November 2017, the following statement:
Decision 8 - 6

1. I have no relationship or conflicts with any of the Parties, in addition to the company/entity referred to
in the Request: [B]. A number of Brazilian subsidiaries of [C] previously held an interest in the
agreement in dispute. I was employed by a […] subsidiary of [C] [for a year]. My understanding is that
neither [C] nor any of its subsidiaries are a party to this dispute.
2. I know a number of counsel representing both the Respondents and the Claimant. A number of them
have spoken at the […] conference that I chair each year or I have spoken on or moderated panels at
arbitration conferences on which some of these counsel have participated. In addition, I am a member
of professional organizations, such as [Organisation D] […], to which some of these counsel are
members also. I do not have a close personal relationship with any of these counsel.
3. I do not know, nor have I had any past or present relationship with, the other party appointed
arbitrator, [E].
4. I do not believe that any of the above circumstances are in conflict with LCIA Arbitration No. […].
However, out of an abundance of caution, I wish to disclose any circumstance that may give rise to the
mind of any party in this LCIA Arbitration any justifiable doubt as to my impartiality or independence."
11. On 16 January 2018 the LCIA wrote to the parties confirming the nomination of the Tribunal and
including [A]’s CV, which quoted his website address. The CV also referred to his work with
[Organisation D] of which he had acted as president.
12. No objection being taken to these matters, [A]'s nomination was confirmed as were those of the other
nominated arbitrators, [E] and [F] as presiding arbitrator.
13. The arbitration was bifurcated by Procedural Order no. 2 and on 24 September 2018, the Phase I
Award was issued by the Arbitral Tribunal. On 2 November 2018, in the course of Phase 2 of the
arbitration, Second Respondent gave notice of its intention to engage new co-counsel.
14. On 6 November 2018, the LCIA sent the Parties a letter from [A] dated 5 November 2018, in which he
made further disclosures regarding his relationship to [G], one of the proposed new co-counsel. [A]
stated that he had known [G] on a personal basis for many years because:
"similar to myself, [G] is a Past President of [Organisation D]. I have therefore worked with him in the
past on various […] committees [of Organisation D] on a pro bono basis".
15. Following this disclosure the Claimant states that it proceeded to conduct further inquiries concerning
[A]. The Claimant sought to ascertain whether [A] had worked at [Law Firm H], a […] law firm, which
had worked for one of the owners of the Second Respondent ([Parent Company I]). The Claimant also
Decision 8 - 7

sought further information on [A]’s work on [Organisation D’s] committees.
16. The Claimant therefore requested further clarifications from [A] as to the nature of his personal
relationship with [G] and as to his working or co-working on [Organisation D] and organizations in
general. [A] was asked to provide more details on the works performed by him in each of the
committees, providing a list of the committees and their respective scopes, the nature of the work
and the periods in which they were performed and whether [A] participated in the drafting of the
[Organisation D] model contract that is the subject of the arbitration, or any of its clauses. [A] was also
requested to confirm the information about his association with [Law Firm H].
17. On 2 January 2019, [A] responded to the Claimant's request disclosing that:
"[for around 3 years], I was [working at] [Law Firm J]. [Law Firm J] had an alliance with [Law Firm H]
during that time period".
He stated also that:
"I do not know of [Parent Company I], nor am I aware of the work that [Law Firm H] may or may not
have done for that corporation".
18. [A] stated that he and [G]:
“were members of the drafting committee for [a] version of the [Organisation D] Model [Agreement].
I was responsible for the drafting of [certain sections] of the [Organisation D] Model [Agreement]" and,
that [A] "was the Vice President [of Organisation D’s committee] [for some years]".
19. The Claimant contends that [Law Firm H] had been legal counsel not only to [Parent Company I] but
also to [Parent Company K], both being the owners of the Second Respondent, and their affiliates.
[Law Firm H] had also, in addition to [Parent Companies I and K], represented other related companies
in some fifteen named transactions or projects, all such companies being either the Second
Respondent's Owners or affiliates.
20. The claimant contends that the foregoing matters call into question [A]'s independence and
impartiality in the arbitration, particularly because [A] worked in a firm that provided services, to and
received substantial fees from, the Second Respondent's Owners; and further in that [A]’s work in the
drafting of the [Organisation D] Model [Agreement] makes him biased to participate on the decision-
making process about the validity of clauses of a contract that was based on that model.
Decision 8 - 8

Claimant’s submissions
21. The Claimant emphasizes the need for parties to have confidence in the impartiality and independence
of arbitrators given the powers vested in them in relation to the disputes referred. Impartiality has
been described as the watchword of all tribunals, including arbitrators, a proposition which is not to
be doubted.
22. Nor is it to be doubted that arbitrators have a heavy duty of disclosure of any information that may
give rise to doubts, in the eyes of the parties, regarding their impartiality. Impartiality is to be judged
objectively and not through the eyes of the arbitrator. The UNCITRAL Rules, applicable in this case,
require by Article 9 that an arbitrator should disclose any circumstance likely to give rise to a justifiable
doubts as to his impartiality or independence and thereafter to disclose any further circumstances not
previously disclosed.
23. Given that the seat of this arbitration is Paris and the procedural law French law, it is relevant to note
that Article 1456 of the French Code of Civil Procedure imposes on the arbitrators the same duty to
disclose any circumstances that could give rise to doubts concerning their impartiality and
independence as provided by the UNCITRAL Rules. Further given that the governing law of the contract
is Brazilian law, the same duty is seen to be recognized by the Brazilian courts in relation to
enforcement of an award2. The duty is found universally, both in Rules and in laws applicable
throughout the world.
First ground of challenge
24. The Claimant’s first ground of challenge is that [A] worked for a firm that is said to have provided
services to, and received substantial fees from, the Second Respondent's Owners. [A] disclosed on
2 January 2018 that he worked for [Law Firm J] which had an association with [Law Firm H]. Further
researches showed that [A] was publicly identified as "[Lawyer] with [Law Firm H]", and his
professional e-mail address was a [Law Firm H] email address.
25. [Law Firm H] has frequently and consistently given advice to the Second Respondent's Owners,
2Abengoa Case STJ; SE 9412/US; Reporter: Min. Felix Fischer; Date of judgement: 30 May 2017.
Decision 8 - 9

especially financial advice. Connections with the parties, in the broad sense, are considered sufficient
to result in lack of independence. In that respect, the IBA Guidelines are deemed to represent
international best practice and are relevant criteria in common as well as civil law jurisdictions when
evaluating the potential independence of an arbitrator. The connection between [A]'s previous law
firm and the Second Respondent's Owners and respective subsidiaries are clear and serious elements
of lack of independence and impartiality pursuant to standards of the IBA Guidelines.
26. The Claimant relies on point 3.1.4 of the Orange List, above, which refers to situations which, in the
opinion of the parties, may give rise to justifiable doubts as to the arbitrator's impartiality or
independence.
27. General Standard 7 of the IBA Guidelines, which was applicable in the present case, required that a
party must inform an arbitrator, other parties and the arbitration institution or appointing authority
of any relationship, direct or indirect, between the arbitrator and the party or another company of the
same group. The party must do so on its own initiative at the earliest opportunity.
28. The same rule further required the arbitrator to make reasonable enquiries to identify any conflict of
interest, as well as any facts or circumstances that may reasonably give rise to doubts as to his or her
impartiality or independence. Further, a failure to disclose a conflict is not excused by lack of
knowledge, if the arbitrator does not perform such reasonable enquiries.
29. Under any standards of international arbitration practice, including the IBA Guidelines and the 1976
UNCITRAL Rules, [A] should have disclosed the fact that he worked in a law firm that provided services
to the two owners of one of the Respondents.
Second ground of challenge
30. [A] disclosed only on 2 January 2019 his participation in the drafting of […] "[a] version of the
[Organisation D] Model [Agreement]". Also, on that date he disclosed that [for some years] he was
the Vice-President of [a committee] for [Organisation D]. He had previously disclosed that he knew
some of the counsel engaged in the arbitration, and that "in addition, I am a member of professional
organizations, such as [Organisation D] […], to which some of these counsel are members also. I do not
have a close personal relationship with any of these counsel". His membership of [Organisation D] was
not disclosed as a potential conflict, nor in particular his special roles with regard to the [Organisation
Decision 8 - 10

D] Model [Agreement].
31. It is common ground that the [Agreement] signed by the Parties is based on the [Organisation
D] Model [Agreement]. [A] clearly knew already that he had constantly participated and watched over,
in several capacities, that very [Organisation D] Model [Agreement]. Therefore, [A] knew that he
would be directly participating in the judgment of the validity of clauses of a contract that he
contributed to develop, which obviously keeps him from being objective towards the legal dispute at
hand.
32. [A] therefore has an interest that the clauses of the contracts based on [Organisation D] Model
[Agreements] are not declared null and void. If not that, then at least [A] is biased as to his personal
belief that those clauses are valid, before even analyzing the case – given his involvement in building
the very contract the validity of which was subject to his scrutiny.
33. Case law has established that if an arbitrator has a standing with respect to a subject, that is
considered grounds to file a challenge. With much more reason, it is clear that if the appointee
contributed to draft the document under dispute, such appointee should not accept to take part in
the tribunal. The [Agreement] was created 'in the image and likeness of' the [Organisation
D] Model [Agreement]. The [Organisation D] Model [Agreement] and the [Agreement] are not
dissociable. A dispute about the validity and effects of one, is a dispute about the other. [A] knew that
by the time he was appointed, and should have made disclosures of all these circumstances.
34. Although the Tribunal declared that trade usages of the oil and gas industry were not relevant to the
conclusions, the Phase I Award spent over 5 of 66 pages discussing, in the context of the oil and gas
industry, the rationale, pertinence, relevance, and appropriateness of the terms of the [Agreement]
[Organisation D] models, which indicates that those matters had influence over the result of the case.
It is unavoidable that [A] contributed to that result, from a privileged position, by definition without
an impartial and independent view.
35. In deciding the challenge, the appointing authority should be guided by the assumption that
arbitrators would not want to contradict themselves. It would be naïve to assume that [A] would help
to draft an [Organisation D] Model [Agreement], be responsible for reviewing and safeguarding the
[Organisation D] Model [Agreement], dedicate significant time and effort to the dissemination of the
Decision 8 - 11

[Organisation D] Model [Agreement], and, then subsequently be objectively open, independent, and
impartial in regards to arguments of third parties (in this case, the Claimant) against the validity and
effects of a document that carbon-copied that model.
36. The IBA Guidelines suggests the perspective to determine the existence of a duty to disclose: "in the
eyes of the parties". This means that the mere fact that an arbitrator may not himself or herself
consider that particular facts call into question his independence does not suffice to justify non-
disclosure. To ensure compliance with the duty of disclosure arbitrators must themselves investigate
the circumstances3.
37. So, it would have been expected from [A] to assume that disclosure of his previous works was required
since they could reasonably call into question his independence "in the eyes of the parties", especially
since the facts at hand fall within the IBA Guidelines Orange List. The mere failure to disclose
information is by itself sufficient for a challenge to be accepted. [A]'s failure to disclose the facts that
gave rise to this challenge should, in and of itself, lead to the acceptance of this challenge.
Conclusion
38. All of the facts above, specially taken together, lead to justifiable doubts as to [A]'s impartiality and
independence to be an arbitrator in this case. Different challenge grounds can reveal a pattern and, if
taken together, they render an arbitrator partial even if each of the issues is not sufficient separately.4
This is because the overall impression is that the arbitrator deviates from the ideal of an impartial and
independent arbitrator who has to ensure a high degree of procedural fairness by upholding these
qualities.
39. The Claimant requests the Tribunal, the LCIA and the appointing authority to take all necessary
measures resulting from this challenge, and from its acceptance, and reserves the right to amend and
make new requests related to this challenge.
Response of Second Respondent
3 General Standard 7(d) of the IBA Guidelines
4 BORN, Garry. International Commercial Arbitration London 2014. Second Edition.p.1866
Decision 8 - 12

40. A Response was submitted by email on 22 January 2019 on behalf of the Second Respondent. In
response to the first ground it is noted that the Claimant’s allegations were based on independent
research following [A]’s letter of 6 November 2018. As the challenge was not filed until 17 January
2019 it is outside the time limits specified in Article 11(1) of the UNCITRAL Rules.
41. As to the substance of the challenge, at the time [A] was nominated by the Respondents, he was not
employed by either [Law Firm H] or [Law Firm J] and the fact that [Law Firm H] may have undertaken
work for the Second Respondent’s investors or companies affiliated to them is irrelevant. It was
further impossible for [A] to obtain any information about [Law Firm H’s] work for the Second
Respondent’s investors or companies affiliated to them or disclose such information, if relevant.
42. In relation to the second ground relied on the fact that [A] was involved in drafting [a version of]
[Organisation D] Model Form [Agreement] does not mean that he has or is likely to have pre-judged
the validity of certain clauses under Brazilian law. If anything [A]’s familiarity with the oil and gas
industries is an asset to the Tribunal. In any event [A]’s work for [Organisation D] and his involvement
in drafting the Model Form Agreements are well-known and were referred to in the LCIA’s letter to
the parties dated 16 January 2018. They are also set out on [A]’s website which was also identified in
the attachment.
Response of First Respondent
43. A Response was submitted on 23 January 2019 on behalf of the First Respondent. It is first challenged
that [A]’s failure to disclose his past interaction with [Law Firm H] and his past involvement with
[Organisation D] is sufficient to raise doubts about his impartiality and independence.
44. Under Articles 9 and 10 of the UNCITRAL Rules and International Arbitration Practice as reflected in
the authorities, a challenge must be based on facts that raise justifiable doubts as to an arbitrator’s
independence and impartiality. Lack of disclosure is not per se sufficient to support a challenge: only
the facts or circumstances not disclosed can do so. The facts as presented by the Claimant do not raise
any justifiable doubts about [A]’s independence or impartiality.
45. [A]’s past association with a firm can have no bearing on his current appointment, [A]’s work with
[Law Firm J] having ceased […] over 2 years before his appointment by the Respondents in the present
arbitration and [A]’s association with [Law Firm H] being at most indirect.
Decision 8 - 13

46. Further, [A]’s involvement with [Organisation D] does not raise any justifiable doubts about his
independence and impartiality. As a threshold matter, the Claimant waived any such challenge when
it failed to conduct the most basic enquiries about [A] and bring its complaint within 15 days from
[A]’s original disclosure as required by Article 11.1 of the UNCITRAL Rules. [A] disclosed his association
with [Organisation D] on 27 November 2017, the 15 day time limit expiring on 12 December 2017.
Further the extent of his involvement with [Organisation D] is a matter of public knowledge disclosed
on [A]’s website and thus easily discoverable through a simple search which the Claimant failed to
make.
47. In any event, [A]’s work as one of the drafters of the […] version of the [Organisation D] Model
[Agreement] is the very expertise the parties look for in arbitrators and constitutes an asset to the
Tribunal and the parties. There is no evidence of any predisposition in the matters in dispute and no
doubts about his impartiality and independence arise. The [Organisation D] [Agreement] is a mere
contractual model which neither reflects any personal belief about any concrete case nor addresses
the issue of the validity of the [Agreement]s clause under Brazilian law.
Response of [A]
48. [A] responded briefly on 19 January 2019 rejecting the challenge. He responded in detail on 28 January
2019 stating, in respect of the first ground of challenge, that his first and only knowledge of the Second
Respondent’s shareholders was when their identity was disclosed by the Claimant in the course of its
challenge. Until then he had never heard of the two companies [Parent Company I] and [Parent
Company K]. In addition he had never dealt with the companies at any time, and was not aware that
[Law Firm H] had provided legal services for these companies until the Claimant disclosed this
information.
49. [A] states that he was employed [for a certain amount of time] by [Law Firm J]and had not been a
partner or an employee of [Law Firm H] at any time. A letter from his previous employer, [Law Firm J]
dated 27 January 2019 is produced confirming that [A]’s practice while employed by [Law Firm J] was
exclusively focussed on that firm’s […] [regional union] clients and their business files. During the term
of his employment the [Law Firm J] had an association with [Law Firm H] to provide legal services in
[…] the Gulf region. As part of the arrangement [Law Firm H] provided IT services including an email
Decision 8 - 14

system. As a result, [A] was required to use [Law Firm H’s] email system to correspond with the firm’s
clients.
50. [A] states that his CV was included in the LCIA’s letter of 16 January 2018 confirming the Tribunal to
all parties in the arbitration. That CV had been published in Who’s Who Legal: Arbitration and also
provided his website details. The website provided information on his relationship with [Organisation
D] including work on development of [Organisation D] Model Contracts and specifically being one of
the drafters of the original [Organisation D] Model […] ([Agreement]). This information was therefore
disclosed or available in January 2018 and was not, as the Claimant’s allege, disclosed only in January
2019. The website also includes a list of [A]’s publications including one article listing [A] as a lawyer
with [Law Firm H]. However, at the time the article was written, [A] was employed by [Law Firm J].
51. As regards the work with the [Organisation D] Model […] Agreement, [A] was not involved in drafting
the [later] version of the Model [Agreement] which is the contract in dispute in the arbitration, nor
was he responsible for drafting the particular provisions of the Model Form being disputed in the
arbitration. [A] states that he did not have a pre-disposition on the validity or enforceability of the
clauses and is aware of published cases that have dealt with similar issues.
Claimant’s Reply to Opposing submission
52. The Claimant’s Reply was filed on 11 February 2019, after an extension granted by the Secretariat. The
Reply first addresses the contention that the challenge was not timely, being submitted outside the
15 day period prescribed. The Claimant disputes the contention, arguing that the challenge is based
not on facts disclosed, but on the facts not disclosed by [A], which non-disclosure continued up to 2
January 2019. The challenge filed on 17 January 2019 was, therefore, timely. In any event the Claimant
cites earlier published decisions on challenges before the LCIA in which a Tribunal in one case decided
that the timing of the challenge was irrelevant to the merits; and in another decision, a 3-member
division of the LCIA was hesitant in dismissing a challenge on the basis of its timing.
53. As regards [A]’s relation with [Law Firm H], what is relevant is whether such relationship, either past
or ongoing, is likely to be seen as affecting an arbitrator’s ability to be impartial and independent. The
relevant test according to the IBA Guidelines and as adopted in other LCIA challenges is whether a
reasonable and informed third party would reach the conclusion that there was a likelihood that the
Decision 8 - 15

56. The Claimant then addresses the “subjective impartiality” of [A] by quoting, in addition to references

to the Tribunal’s decision in the Phase I award5 references to the transcript of the hearing in which it

Discussion and conclusions
58. The starting point must be to re-state the standard of independence and impartiality required of
arbitrators and the appropriate formulation of the duty that falls upon arbitrators in this regard. It is,
of course, not to be doubted that impartiality is of the highest importance and that it is to be judged
objectively. At the same time, it must be remembered that there is an ongoing debate as to the extent
to which arbitrators must also be “independent” and as to the appropriate meaning to be given to
that somewhat imprecise concept. It is of some note that the English Arbitration Act 1996 eschews
the word “independent” and opts instead for “impartial”, on the basis that arbitrators are generally
expected to have experience of the particular trade or profession which gives rise to the dispute, and
that fact alone makes it likely that arbitrators will have had, in their past, some connection with or at
least knowledge of the parties and others involved in an arbitration, including expert witnesses and
counsel.
5 Claimant’s challenge para. 88.
Decision 8 - 17

59. Thus, the mere fact that some connection may exist between an arbitrator and the parties or
personnel involved in an arbitration is not of itself a matter of criticism and is unlikely of itself to be
sufficient to disqualify a prospective arbitrator. The appropriate test against which an alleged lack of
impartiality is to be judged is that of an objective third party having all the relevant knowledge about
the case and about the circumstances of the challenged arbitrator. The question is whether such a
third party would regard the matters relied on as creating real or justifiable doubt as to the impartiality
of that arbitrator. The test is expressed in the IBA Guidelines in terms of particular practical
circumstances. But these are all subject to the overriding general rule (as also expressed in the IBA
Guidelines) that the matters relied upon in any challenge must be such as to give rise, in the eyes of
an informed and independent third party, to justifiable doubt as to the arbitrator’s impartiality.
60. As an additional issue which might be seen as part of the overall test, the Claimant seeks to rely on
the very fact of non-disclosure as “of itself” giving rise to justifiable doubts as to impartiality,
irrespective of the facts relied on, a contention denied by the opposing parties. This can be disposed
of at the outset since, in my view, such an argument is circular and cannot add anything to the basic
test as outlined above. If the facts relied on are themselves insufficient to ground a proper challenge,
then the failure to disclose those facts cannot “of itself” generate a further ground of challenge
separate from those facts.
61. In considering the broad test to be applied is also useful to have regard to the more detailed rules as
set out in the IBA Guidelines and the UNCITRAL Rules. Both the Guidelines and the Rules contain time
limits within which a challenge should be brought, the limit under the Rules being 15 days and that
under the Guidelines 30 days after the party intending to mount a challenge becomes aware of the
circumstances relied on. The so-called “Orange List” of grounds of challenge, which are “waivable”,
are deemed to have been waived if the party who has the right to challenge on such a ground does
not do so within the prescribed number of days. While the notion of ruling out a challenge on such a
ground is unattractive, there is a more important point underlying the rules in that time is to be
regarded as significant.
62. In regard to the specific ground relied on in relation to [Law Firm H], the basis of the challenge is that
the arbitrator’s law firm has “within the past 3 years” acted for or against one of the parties or an
affiliate of one of the parties in an unrelated matter without the involvement of the arbitrator. The
point to be made here is that the ground of challenge is deemed to expire after 3 years. The same
Decision 8 - 18

principle is applied (under Rule 3.1.1) in relation to an arbitrator having served as counsel for one of
the parties or an affiliate of one of the parties or previously advising in an unrelated matter (in the
absence of an ongoing relationship). Again, the available ground of challenge is deemed to expire after
3 years.
63. In the present case the period of time between the occurrence of the event relied on (which
terminated upon [A] leaving [Law Firm J] in July 2015) and the appointment of the Tribunal (in January
2018) is some 2½ years and thus within the 3 year period under the rule. However, it must be relevant
that had the arbitration commenced some 6 months later, or had [A] terminated his employment
earlier in January 2015, the events relied on would not have fallen within paragraph 3.1.4 of the
Guidelines at all. It seems obvious that the 3 year period stated in the IBA Guidelines is a somewhat
arbitrary period. But the underlying principle which it expresses is that the effluxion of time is to be
regarded as curative in respect of such contended conflicts. It follows that, unlike a statutory period
of limitation, there is good reason to take into account the period of time that has elapsed between
the situation relied on as creating the conflict and the date of the arbitrator’s appointment. In short,
it is a relevant consideration that the event relied on was close to being cured by the passing of time.
64. Turning to the specific ground relied on in relation to [A]’s employment with [Law Firm J], it must be
accepted that that firm had a close relationship with [Law Firm H] which in turn had acted during the
period of [A]’s employment for the associated companies [Parent Company I] and [Parent Company
K] or for other associates of the Second Respondents, for which advice was provided and fees received.
Such an association falls either within or, bearing in mind that [A] worked for a different law firm, very
close to ground 3.1.4 of the Orange List and thus entitled the Claimant to mount the present challenge.
However, even where the facts fall squarely within the stated ground of challenge, disqualification is
not automatic and, as the general standards state, the outcome depends on the particular facts. The
question to be decided is whether those facts give rise, viewed objectively, to justifiable doubts as to
the arbitrator’s impartiality. It should be added that while [A] did have a duty to investigate and to
disclose those circumstances, as already stated, the fact of non-disclosure cannot of itself add to the
weight to be given to the relevant facts.
65. The contrary case put forward on behalf of the Respondents and [A] himself, as already anticipated,
is that the relevant facts ceased to apply some 2½ years before [A]’s appointment. To this may be
Decision 8 - 19

added the fact that [A], despite appearances to the contrary, in fact worked for [Law Firm J] and not
for [Law Firm H] and there has been no suggestion that [A]’s work for [Law Firm J] was in any way
connected with the engagement of [Law Firm H] by the Second Respondent’s owners or affiliates.
66. As regards the prospective arbitrator’s duty of investigation, [A] states that he had never heard of the
companies in question and was unaware of any possible conflict arising from those circumstances.
While there may be a duty to investigate whether a law firm for which a prospective arbitrator has
worked in the past has acted for the parties to the case or for known associates of those companies,
it is difficult to see how the duty could extend to companies of which the prospective arbitrator is
unaware. [A] could not, 2½ years after his employment ended, ask for a list of every company for
which [Law Firm H] had provided advice in the past. Such information would in any event be
confidential. There is therefore considerable doubt as to whether [A] breached any obligation of
disclosure.
67. The Claimant in its Reply Submissions seeks to emphasise the significance of [A]’s earlier employment
and its connections with the Second Respondent including the fact that [A] must be taken to have
received some financial benefit as a result of the work carried out for those companies. In my view
these observations are simply part of the relationship which is the subject of paragraph 3.1.4 of the
Guidelines and do not add significantly to it. Ultimately, it is a matter of objective judgment as to
whether the facts established are such as to give rise to justifiable doubts as to [A]’s ability to act as a
member of the arbitral tribunal.
68. In my view, taking into account particularly the length of time that has elapsed since [A]’s employment,
the tentative nature of the connection between [A] and the relevant companies and [A]’s ignorance
of the companies in question, the facts relied on do not justify the conclusion that [A] on this account
lacked impartiality.
69. With regard the second ground of challenge, the Claimant emphasizes [A]’s involvement in drafting
the [later] version of the [Agreement] Model and the fact that he was chair of [a committee] when a
new [Agreement] Model was issued [even later on]. [A] in fact states that he was not involved in
drafting the […] version which is the Contract in dispute in the present arbitration. He adds that he
was not responsible for drafting the particular provisions of the Model Form being disputed in the
arbitration. [A] accepts that he was one of the drafters of the [earlier] Model […] Agreement, which
Decision 8 - 20

was disclosed on [A]’s website which also included a list of his publications. [A] thus denies that he
was responsible for drafting the particular provisions of the Model Form being disputed in this
arbitration.
70. Whatever [A]’s actual involvement in the drafting of the Form of Contract under review in the
arbitration, as a matter of common experience with institutional bodies, it cannot be the case that [A]
was solely responsible for any part of the Form. Such documents are invariably drafted in committee
with appropriate legal input as the drafting proceeds. Once a standard form is produced it is, from
time to time, reviewed and new editions issued, as is the case here. To contend that [A], whether as
Vice President, President or simply a member of the drafting body was himself the draftsman of a
particular provision is unrealistic. At the highest, [A] would have had knowledge of the background
and the policy considerations behind the drafting of successive versions of the standard form and
would, of course, have had a detailed knowledge of the content of the successive versions of the
standard form as they were produced.
71. The question is whether [A]’s past involvement and familiarity with Model [Agreement] forms is such
as to disqualify him from adjudicating on a dispute involving a version of those forms. There is no
doubt that, as the Respondents contend, such involvement and familiarity is a positive advantage and
could be seen as the very quality which the parties seek in an arbitrator. But the question is whether,
in the present case, the degree of involvement was such as to impair [A]’s impartiality and
independence. It may be noted that the same question will arise in respect of standard forms and
documentation in other industries where contractual and technical disputes often involve standard
forms in which many individuals will have had involvement through professional institutions. Are all
such individuals to be regarded as disqualified through their involvement?
72. It is to be noted that the relevant events, starting with [A]’s involvement with the [earlier] version of
the Model [Agreement], occurred well over 20 years before his appointment in the present case. It is
also to be noted that [A]’s involvement with [Organisation D] was disclosed in his original statement
of independence of November 2017. Further details were readily available on [A]’s website which
were freely disclosed and available. The Claimant subsequently requested many more details of [A]’s
work. But it is fair to say that the Claimant’s more recent interest in [A]’s detailed involvement in
drafting has been generated by the outcome of the first hearing and the Tribunal’s award. [A]’s
involvement in drafting of the forms and documents which were in issue in the arbitration could have
Decision 8 - 21

been the subject of further enquiry of [A] himself upon his nomination. I do not regard [A]’s detailed
involvement in drafting committees as a matter which should have been disclosed once his
involvement with [Organisation D] was on the record. All the information subsequently disclosed by
[A] concerning his involvement with [Organisation D] could have been requested by the Claimant if
thought of relevance, but no such request was made.
73. The provisions of the UNCITRAL Rules regarding time and waiver have already been discussed above.
The underlying principle is that a party may not subsequently raise complaints concerning issues which
were known at the date of appointment and the same must apply in respect of matters which were
readily or at least reasonably available had the party seeking to mount the challenge made appropriate
investigation. In the present case, and given the remoteness of [A]’s involvement in the original
drafting of the Model [Agreement] Form, I do not consider that [A] failed in a material respect as
regards his duty of disclosure.
74. The Claimant’s attempt in its Reply submission to present, from the hearing transcript, a picture of [A]
as being strongly committed to the validity of the contractual provisions of the [Organisation D] Model
Form and of revealing pre-conceptions and a lack of partiality is unconvincing. The references quoted
from the transcript cannot be properly evaluated without reviewing the full hearing record and, as
anticipated by the Claimant, introducing evidence. Such a procedure is beyond the scope of the
present inquiry in which the Claimant has the burden of putting before this Tribunal sufficient material
from which it can be concluded that the relief sought should be granted. For the avoidance of doubt
the Claimant’s request for a further hearing is refused.
75. Taking into account all the matters reviewed above, I regard the length of time that has elapsed since
[A]’s involvement in drafting the standard forms to be such as to render any prejudice to the Claimant
of questionable significance. Of even more relevance is that his involvement with [Organisation D] was
disclosed along with his website where further details were readily available. If further information as
to his work in [the earlier version] and thereafter with [Organisation D] was regarded as relevant it
could have been requested on his nomination, but was not. For all these reasons I have come to the
conclusion that the second ground of challenge fails.
